AnkiMobile Manual

# Study Tools

The tools screen will open when you tap on the gear/cog icon in the study screen. On the top right, there are buttons that will adjust the text size on your cards. The “Frequent Actions” section contains some commonly used actions. You can rearrange the actions there or remove actions by holding your finger on a button for a second or so. Below the “Frequent Actions” section is a list of all available actions in AnkiMobile. You can add these actions to the “Frequent Actions” section by long-pressing on them.

## Actions
The following actions can be run from the tools screen, or by assigning them to a tap, swipe, or the top bar in the preferences. Add
Opens a new window to add cards to the deck. Answer “Again”

When the answer screen is shown, choose the red button, indicating you wish to review the card again soon. This is useful when you forgot a card or wish to review it more frequently. Answer “Hard”

When the answer screen is shown and there are four buttons, choose the second button from the left, indicating you found the card hard to remember. Answer “Good”

When the answer screen is shown, choose the green button. This is the button you should end up using the most. Answer “Easy”

When the answer screen is shown, choose the button on the right, indicating you found the card too easy to remember and would like a much longer delay.

results.summary:
# Hard/good interval is longer than good/easy

When a card is in learning:

- Again will be the first learning step
- Hard will repeat the current learning step (except on the first step, where it is the average of first and second steps)
- Good will the the next learning step, or the Graduating interval if learning steps are exhausted
- Easy will be the Easy Interval

Now that I have explained what happens if we click / type on the Good button, I will proceed to explain what happens if we click Again, Hard or Easy. As it can be seen in the Figure 15, the formula is different.

Again button algorithm: current interval * new interval %. Ease -20%

The current interval of days that we have for each card is multiplied by the New interval set in the Lapses section, in the Figure 18. The default option is 0%, which means that if we have answered incorrectly a “learnt card”, no matter the current interval of days (10 days or even 10 years), the next time that we will see the card will be the “Steps (in minutes)” of the Lapses section (it is important not to confuse with the Steps in the New Cards section). Then, once we have answered correctly again, the current interval will be the New interval, which by default is set to 0% of the previous one, that is to say, the Minimum interval. Of course, both the Minimum interval and the New interval can be changed.

For example, in my personal configuration I have the New interval at 50%. If I failed a flashcard with a current interval of 1.5 years, the next time I would see it would be the Steps (in minutes), which I have configurated in 20 minutes, and the next time, if answered correctly, in 0.75 years, and then it would continue with the Anki algorithm in the Figure 15. This modification has helped me avoiding concentration mistakes that could made me lose big streaks. For example, with a streak of 1.5 years, I should have already interiorized the word quite well. It could happen that I was tired in the moment of studying and pressed “Show answer” too early, and then when I saw the answer I could think “Of course, I knew it!” This happens frequently when using Anki a lot. Thus, it may be worthwhile increasing the default New interval of 0% to a higher %.

Finally, the Ease of the card is reduced to 20% (reminding: default starting ease = 250% and the minimum is 130%) but this happens ONLY if the card was already graduated.

results.title: How to Use Anki: A Step-by-Step Guide for Beginners
results.summary:
the deck options manual(opens in a new tab) estimates that 20 new cards a day settles into roughly 200 reviews a day, and Anki's own tooltip says the new-card limit should be at least 10 times smaller than the review limit. The review limit caps new cards too: with a limit of 200 and 190 reviews due, Anki adds at most 10.

Short on time? Start with 10. Changes apply to every deck sharing the preset (new decks use Default).

## Anki FSRS settings

FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler) has been built into Anki since version 23.10(opens in a new tab), released in October 2023. Per the manual, it is an alternative to the older SM-2 algorithm that predicts more accurately when you'll forget each card, so it can help you remember more in the same study time. A new collection starts with FSRS off, so switch it on:

- Open Deck Options (gear icon, then Options).
- Scroll to the FSRS section at the bottom and turn FSRS on. It applies to your whole collection.
- Leave Desired retention at its default of 90%.
- Keep your Learning steps under 1 day; the default 1m 10m is fine.
- Click Save.
- After a few hundred reviews, click Optimize Current Preset to fit FSRS to your own history. Once a month is plenty.

Three cautions from the manual's FSRS section(opens in a new tab):

- Every device you sync must support FSRS: Anki or AnkiMobile 23.10+, AnkiWeb, or AnkiDroid 2.17+.
- Higher retention means more reviews. Workload climbs quickly above 90%, so stay below 97%.
- FSRS treats Hard as a pass, so pressing Hard on a forgotten card inflates its intervals.

Converting an existing collection? Leave Reschedule cards on change off at first. For how FSRS compares with SM-2, see our FSRS guide.

## How to use Anki shared decks

AnkiWeb's shared deck library(opens in a new tab) offers ready-made decks in categories such as languages, anatomy, chemistry, history, and law.

- On the Decks screen, click Get Shared.
- Search or pick a category, open a deck, and click Download to get an.apkg file.
- Double-click the file, or use File > Import in Anki.
- Leave Import any learning progress unticked, so you don't inherit the author's intervals (an option since Anki 23.10(opens in a new tab)).

Shared decks can't go straight into AnkiWeb; import them into Anki, AnkiMobile, or AnkiDroid, then sync. The manual(opens in a new tab) treats them as a supplement: great for list-like facts such as capitals and flags, or a deck built around your textbook, but for complex subjects your own cards carry context that someone else's lack.

## How to use Anki image occlusion

Image Occlusion has been built into Anki since 23.10(opens in a new tab), so no add-on is needed. It masks parts of an image, such as the labels on an anatomy diagram, and quizzes you on each one.

- Click Add, click the note type button at the top left (labeled Type), and choose Image Occlusion.
- Click Select Image, or Paste Image from Clipboard if you copied one.
- Draw a rectangle, ellipse, or polygon over each label you want to hide.
- Pick a mode: Hide All, Guess One keeps every label covered, while Hide One, Guess One covers only the label being tested.
...
Anki creates one card per shape or group of shapes.

## How to sync Anki with AnkiWeb

AnkiWeb is Anki's free sync service, and you can also study on it in a browser.

- Create a free account at ankiweb.net(opens in a new tab).
- In Anki on your computer, click Sync at the top right of the main window (or press Y) and sign in with your AnkiWeb email and password.
- On the first sync, choose Upload to AnkiWeb if your cards are on this computer, or Download from AnkiWeb if they're already in your account.
- Sign in on your phone with the same account and sync there too.

New (Blue): Cards you have added to your deck but have never studied before.

By default, a limit applies to how many of these you see daily, though this can be adjusted in deck options.

Learning/Relearning (Red/Orange): cards being learned

Due (Green): cards you’ve learned already that are due for review

## Anki Mobile

By default, cards show center aligned. To set to left aligned, go to any deck, click the ⚙️ icon on the bottom right corner. Under “All Actions”, go to “Card Template”. Choose “CSS Styling” on the bottom of the screen. Now, where it says “text-align: center;”, replace “center” with “left”.

Left side of screen is again, and right side is good. This allows you to tap on the left side of the screen to trigger the red button, and the right side of the screen to trigger the green button. Taps near the middle of the screen will be ignored.

### 2. Understanding Intervals and Learning Steps

I think there might be a bit of confusion between intervals and learning steps:

- Intervals: These are used after a card leaves the learning phase. Anki uses an algorithm to calculate the next review interval based on your responses.
- Learning steps: These apply while the card is still learning. For example, if your steps are set to1m 20m 1d 10d, this doesn’t mean the “Again” button shows 10 minutes or the “Easy” button jumps straight to 10 days.
Instead:
- Each time you press Good, the card moves to the next step.
- Hard and Easy can slow down or speed up the progress a bit.

# Anki Deck-Specific First Step

A custom scheduling script for Anki that allows you to configure deck-specific first learning steps for new cards.

## Overview

Anki's default learning steps configuration doesn't allow you to set a custom interval for the first "Hard" button press on new cards. This script solves that limitation by enabling deck-specific configuration of the first learning step for "Again", "Hard", and "Good" buttons on new cards.

### Default Behavior

In Anki's default Learning Steps configuration (e.g., `1m 10m`), when you press buttons on a new card:

  * **Again** : Returns to the first step (1m)
  * **Hard** : Uses the average of the first two steps (6m = (1+10)/2)
  * **Good** : Moves directly to the second step (10m)

The limitation is that you cannot customize the first "Hard" or "Good" intervals independently, and you cannot set different first intervals for different decks. See the Anki documentation on Learning Steps for more information.

## Features

  * Configure the first learning step for "Again", "Hard", and "Good" buttons on new cards (including the first "Hard" step, which Anki's default settings don't support)
  * Set deck-specific first step intervals
  * Automatically applies to new cards only
  * Supports sub-deck matching (sub-decks inherit parent deck settings)
  * Works with Anki's filtered decks and rescheduling

## Installation

  1. Copy the contents of `custom_scheduling.js`
  2. Open Deck Options in Anki using one of these methods: 
    * Click the gear icon on the Decks screen
    * Select a deck and click **Options** at the bottom
    * Click **More > Options** while in review mode
    * Press **O** while in review mode
  3. Navigate to the **Advanced** section
  4. Scroll down to find the **Custom Scheduling** field
  5. Paste the script into the Custom Scheduling field
  6. Click **OK** to save

**Note:** Custom Scheduling is a global option, so the code applies to all presets. See the Anki documentation for more details.

## Configuration

Edit the `deckStepConfig` array to add or modify deck configurations:

    {
        deckName: "ALL::Learning::日本語::Expression",  // Full deck path
        againMins: 0.34,   // First "Again" step in minutes
        hardMins: 6.7,     // First "Hard" step in minutes
        goodMins: 67.32    // First "Good" step in minutes
    }

### Notes

  * Deck names must match exactly (case-sensitive)
  * Sub-decks are matched by prefix, so a sub-deck will inherit its parent's configuration
  * Only affects **new cards** \- existing cards in learning/review are not modified
  * Only configures the **first** learning step for each button - subsequent steps follow Anki's default learning steps configuration
  * First step durations are specified in minutes and converted to seconds automatically

## Example

For a deck named `ALL::
...
Expression`:

  * Clicking "Again" on a new card will schedule it for review in ~20 seconds (0.34 minutes)
  * Clicking "Hard" will schedule it for ~6.7 minutes
  * Clicking "Good" will schedule it for ~67 minutes
